solution.description: Look at one term such as 1/(7 times 8) and notice its shape: any 1/(n(n+1)) splits into 1/n minus 1/(n+1), and that split is what will make the whole series collapse.

solution.operation: Write out the series with partial fractions
solution.description: Rewrite every term with that split, so the series becomes (1/7 - 1/8) + (1/8 - 1/9) + (1/9 - 1/10) + (1/10 - 1/11) and onward.
The cancellation is now visible: the minus 1/8 of the first bracket kills the plus 1/8 of the second, the minus 1/9 kills the plus 1/9, and so on down the chain.
Once every interior fraction has cancelled, all that remains is the opening 1/7 minus whatever fraction the tail leaves behind, which for an endless series is 1/n as n grows without bound.
That trailing fraction shrinks towards 0 as n increases, so in the limit nothing at all is left to subtract from 1/7.
Taking 0 away from 1/7 leaves 1/7 as the sum of the entire infinite series, reached without adding a single pair of fractions directly.

Treating the tail 1/n as a small amount still to be subtracted; for the infinite series it goes to 0 and the sum is exactly 1/7.

concept.technique_name: Vedic Summation of Series (Telescoping by pattern recognition)

examples.problem_statement: Find the sum of the first four terms of the series: $$\frac{1}{7 \times 8} + \frac{1}{8 \times 9} + \frac{1}{9 \times 10} + \frac{1}{10 \times 11}$$

solution.description: Notice that every term has the shape 1/(n(n+1)), and any such term splits into 1/n minus 1/(n+1); this decomposition is what makes the four-term sum collapse.
Split the first term: 1/(7 times 8) becomes 1/7 minus 1/8.
Split the second term the same way: 1/(8 times 9) becomes 1/8 minus 1/9, whose leading 1/8 is already the opposite of the 1/8 left over by the first term.
Split the third term: 1/(9 times 10) becomes 1/9 minus 1/10.
Split the fourth and last term: 1/(10 times 11) becomes 1/10 minus 1/11.
Write the four decomposed terms out in a single line so that the opposing fractions stand side by side.
Cancel each interior pair - the two 1/8s, the two 1/9s and the two 1/10s all vanish - leaving only the opening 1/7 and the closing 1/11.
Put 1/7 minus 1/11 over the common denominator 77, giving 11/77 minus 7/77, which is 4/77, the sum of the four terms.

Here each numerator is exactly the difference of the two binomials in its own denominator, as x minus y sits over (a+x)(a+y); consecutive terms therefore cancel and only the outermost pair survives, leaving x minus w over (a+x)(a+w).

Check the same signature in the numerators: 1 is 8 minus 7, 2 is 10 minus 8, and 14 is 24 minus 10. Because each numerator is its own denominator gap, the chain telescopes to the outer difference 17 over (x+7)(x+24).

The numerators 3, 9, 27 and 99 are again the gaps between successive binomials - 10 minus 7, 19 minus 10, 46 minus 19, 145 minus 46 - so everything between the two ends cancels and the sum is 138 over (x+7)(x+145).

Written in letters, the same cancellation holds with px in place of x, so the three terms sum to a minus d over (px+a)(px+d). This is the general rule that the numerical cases above were instances of.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Remember: The characteristic peculiarity is that each numerator is the difference between the two Binomial factors of its Denominator.'}
{'point': 'Both the Algebraical explanations hereof are exactly as before (and need not be repeated here).'}
{'point': 'Use the Anyayoreva formula for rapid summation.'}
common_mistakes: Applying the shortcut when the numerators are not the gaps between their denominators' binomials; the rule needs 14 to be 24 minus 10, and so on for every term.
Writing only the difference of the outer numbers and forgetting that the surviving denominator is the product of the two outermost binomials.
Leaving the finite answer as 1/7 minus 1/11 rather than combining it over 77 to get 4/77.

concept.technique_name: first differential as the sum of the binomial factors

examples.problem_statement: As regards the quadratic expression x²—5x+6, we know its binomial factors are (x—2) and (x—3).

solution.operation: Identify the quadratic expression and its factors
solution.description: Start from the quadratic x squared minus 5x plus 6 together with its known factorisation into (x - 2) and (x - 3); both forms are needed to see the relationship being demonstrated.

solution.operation: Recall the definition of D₁ for quadratic expressions
solution.description: Set up D1, the first differential of that quadratic, because the claim to be tested is about how D1 relates to those two binomial factors.

solution.operation: Apply the power rule of differentiation
solution.description: Differentiate the leading term: by the power rule, x squared becomes 2x.
Differentiate the middle term: minus 5x has a constant slope, so it contributes minus 5.
Differentiate the constant 6, which contributes nothing at all.
Add the three pieces together to obtain D1 equal to 2x minus 5 for this quadratic.

Now add the two binomial factors instead: (x - 2) plus (x - 3) is also 2x minus 5, confirming that for a quadratic with leading coefficient 1 the first differential is simply the sum of its binomial factors.

Carrying the constant 6 into D1; the derivative of a constant is 0, so D1 is 2x minus 5.
Assuming the sum-of-factors shortcut holds when the coefficient of x squared is not 1; it is stated here for the monic form.

examples.problem_statement: Suppose we have to solve the equation : $\frac{2}{x+2}+\frac{3}{x+3}=\frac{4}{x+4}+\frac{1}{x+1}$

solution.description: Read the equation as it stands: two fractions on each side, each one carrying as its numerator the very constant that appears inside its own denominator.

solution.operation: Apply Śūnyam Anyat (If one is in ratio, the other is zero)
solution.description: That matching of numerator to denominator is the pattern the sutra looks for. The test to run is whether the denominators on the left add to the same expression as the denominators on the right, because when those two sums agree the common sum may be set to zero.

solution.operation: Calculate sum of denominators on left side
solution.description: Add the left-hand denominators: (x+2) plus (x+3) comes to 2x plus 5.

solution.operation: Calculate sum of denominators on right side
solution.description: Add the right-hand denominators: (x+4) plus (x+1) also comes to 2x plus 5, so the condition the sutra requires is met.

solution.operation: Apply Sāmya Samuccaye (When the sums are equal, that sum is zero)
solution.description: Because the two sums are identical, set that common sum equal to zero, which reduces the whole rational equation to the single line 2x plus 5 equals 0.
Solve that linear equation to get x equal to minus 5/2, the root the sutra delivers with no cross-multiplication at all.
Look for the second root by inspection: at x equal to 0 every fraction becomes its numerator over the same number, so both sides read 1 plus 1, and x = 0 satisfies the equation as well.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Remember: For this special type of quadratic, use the "Śūnyam Anyat" formula (one root is zero) and the "Sāmya Samuccaye" Sūtra (sum of denominators equals zero) for the second root.'}
{'point': 'Caution: Recognize the characteristic pattern using the two tests provided.'}
{'point': 'Speed tip: Apply these Vedic Sutras directly once the pattern is identified; no cross-multiplication needed.'}
common_mistakes: Adding the numerators instead of the denominators; the condition that fires here is that both denominator sums come to 2x plus 5.
Stopping at x = -5/2 and missing x = 0, which also satisfies the equation because each fraction reduces to 1.
Cross-multiplying all four fractions into one large polynomial, which throws away the saving the sutra exists to provide.
